# The Country of Night

Shortly before dawn on January 17, 1994, the ground beneath Los Angeles broke. The Northridge earthquake, magnitude 6.7, snapped power lines across the San Fernando Valley, and for the first time in decades the city went truly, totally dark — no streetlamps, no billboards, no amber dome of glow pressing down on the rooftops. Residents stumbled outside in their pajamas, and in the following minutes emergency dispatchers fielded a strange category of call, according to the story that has been passed around ever since: people reporting an enormous, luminous, silvery cloud suspended over the city. Something unnatural. Possibly dangerous. Definitely unprecedented. The cloud, dispatchers explained, was the Milky Way. Some of those callers were adults who had lived their entire lives directly beneath it without ever once seeing it.

We usually tell the history of artificial light as an uncomplicated triumph, and in large part it is. But the conquest of night has been so thorough, so rapid, that we have forgotten night was once a country of its own — with a geography, a jurisdiction, a native population, a set of customs. We did not merely illuminate it. In many ways we annexed it, paved it, and renamed it. What follows is a short account of what that country was like, what happened to it, and why it might be worth keeping a little of it wild.

* * *

When the sun went down for most of human history, most people simply stopped. Not out of virtue, but arithmetic. Light was expensive. A tallow candle — rendered animal fat, smelling faintly of burnt grease, guttering and smoking — cost real money and delivered a fraction of the light of a single hundred-watt bulb. Beeswax burned sweeter and steadier, and was priced accordingly, reserved for churches and the parlors of the wealthy. The poor made do with rushlights, splinters of resinous pine, the coals of the hearth, and whatever the moon chose to give. After dark, the average household went dim, and then went dark.

And yet night was not an absence. It was an institution. The word *curfew* comes from *couvre-feu* — "cover the fire" — the evening bell that marked the official border between day's law and night's law. Gates closed. Watchmen patrolled, calling out the hours so that no one lost track in the black. Medieval courts treated nighttime crime differently from daytime crime, as though darkness were a separate legal territory with its own rules of evidence. Folklore agreed: the nightmare was originally a demon, the *mare*, who sat on sleepers' chests; revenants walked; the dead kept appointments after midnight. Night belonged, provisionally, to the other team.

But terror was only half its economy. Harvesters worked late under the harvest moon, whose extra light existed — agronomically speaking — to bring the crops in. Women spun thread by firelight, which is where the word *spinster* comes from: night was the textile industry's shift. Neighbors visited by moonlight, courted, gossiped, told stories, because in the dark a face disappears and a voice acquires unusual authority. Night was slower than day, poorer in information, and richer in attention.

The strangest custom of that country, though, is the one we have entirely erased. The historian Roger Ekirch spent years digging through diaries, letters, court depositions, and medical texts spanning centuries, and he kept finding the same peculiar phrase, in English, French, Italian: *first sleep*. *Premier sommeil.* *Primo sonno.* Chaucer's characters wake "at the first sleep." The documents reveal a rhythm we would now find bizarre: people did not sleep in one continuous block. They slept for roughly four hours, rose into a drowsy, deliberate interval of an hour or two, and then went back down for a *second* sleep until dawn. In between, they prayed. They pondered their dreams, which were considered communications worth interpreting. They talked, smoked, visited, made love — physicians of the era recommended the interval as the best time to conceive — and occasionally slipped out to commit small, opportunistic thefts. French even had a word for that hovering state: *dorvelle*, asleep and awake at once.

Decades after Ekirch noticed the pattern, a sleep researcher named Thomas Wehr ran an experiment that accidentally recreated the lost world. Volunteers were given fourteen hours of darkness a day for weeks — a simulation of winter light as our ancestors lived it — and their sleep spontaneously split into two phases, separated by a quiet interval of wakefulness. Blood tests showed elevated prolactin during that interval, a hormonal profile closer to meditation than to ordinary alertness. Subjects described it as a serene, liminal state they had never encountered in normal life. Historians debate whether biphasic sleep was truly universal, but the laboratory result is suggestive: the midnight hour may have been a real room in the house of the mind, and we demolished it without recording what it was for. Electric light plus the alarm clock compresses sleep into a single dense block. We enter it late, drugged with screens, and exit abruptly into noise.

* * *

The conquest came in waves. Gaslight arrived first: London's Pall Mall was lit by it in 1807, and by mid-century the industrial cities were veined with gas mains, each district flickering awake as the lamplighter made his rounds with a long pole. Streets acquired nightlife — theaters, cafés, promenading crowds, the flâneur. Paris earned its title as the City of Light. Crime did not vanish, but the balance of the night shifted from dread to commerce.

Meanwhile, the deeper revolution was happening at sea. The nineteenth century's preferred illuminant was whale oil — above all, spermaceti, the waxy substance harvested from the heads of sperm whales, which burned brighter and cleaner than any plant-based rival. Fleets sailed out of New Bedford and Nantucket and chased whales across every ocean, hunting them nearly to extinction so that the drawing rooms of Boston and London could stay lit past sunset. Then, in 1859, drillers in Pennsylvania struck "rock oil," and kerosene — cheaper, abundant, drawn from the ground instead of the sea — undercut whale oil almost overnight. It is one of history's bitter ironies that petroleum probably saved the whale from total annihilation, at least temporarily.

Edison's practical bulb followed in 1879; Pearl Street Station in Manhattan began selling electricity to fifty-nine customers in 1882. From there the timeline collapses. Within a generation, night was negotiable. Within two, it was optional. Within three, it was effectively abolished for anyone living under a city's halo. And no honest person wants to uninvent this. Cheap light is one of civilization's genuine miracles: surgeons operate at three in the morning, children read after chores, factories hum around the clock, and a woman walking home is, on balance, safer under a lamp. The question was never whether the light was good. The question is whether anyone counted what the darkness had been doing for us while we replaced it.

Our bodies, for one, have been filing complaints. Inside your brain sits a gland the size of a grain of rice whose entire job is to wait for nightfall and secrete melatonin, the hormone that opens the door to sleep. Except nightfall rarely arrives anymore. Buried in the retina, alongside the rods and cones, are specialized cells that do nothing but measure ambient brightness and report it to the master clock; they are exquisitely sensitive to blue-white wavelengths — precisely the spectrum of the efficient LEDs now blazing from every ceiling, tablet, and phone. So we lie in bed bathed in spectral noon, informing our bodies it is midday, and wonder why sleep will not come. Millions of people work overnight shifts against this biology; the World Health Organization classifies "shift work involving circadian disruption" as a probable human carcinogen. Researchers talk about "social jet lag" — the chronic mismatch between what the clock demands and what the body expects — as though we were all flying, nightly, across several time zones without going anywhere.

And beneath the measurable damage lies the subtler loss: the interval. Wehr's volunteers found, in the space between their two sleeps, a mode of thought that modern schedules simply never permit — a reverie, half dream and half deliberation, where the night's images could be turned over and examined. Our ancestors used it to interpret dreams, pray, and think unhurried thoughts. We snooze through it. Somewhere in the genome there is presumably still a capacity for that state, like a sealed-off room in an old house, boarded shut and forgotten.

* * *

Above the cities, the losses are easier to photograph. In 2016, researchers published a new world atlas of artificial sky brightness, and its findings read like an elegy: more than eighty percent of humanity lives under light-polluted skies; the Milky Way is hidden from a third of all people on Earth — including roughly eighty percent of North Americans and sixty percent of Europeans. Worse, the trend is steepening. Citizen-science data collected by thousands of stargazers suggest that skyglow is brightening by roughly ten percent a year, which means the number of visible stars is quietly halving within a single childhood. A child born in a major city today may grow up sincerely believing the Milky Way is a candy bar — never learning that the name once referred to actual milk, spilled across heaven by the goddess Hera in the Greek telling; or the Silver River that separates the Weaver Girl from her cowherd in Chinese legend, crossable only once a year over a bridge of magpies; or, in Aboriginal Australian traditions, the Emu, traced not in stars but in the dark dust lanes between them. Every culture that ever lived painted its imagination onto that backdrop. It was the shared canvas of the species.

Professional astronomers have responded the way any displaced people do: by retreating. The great observatories now cluster in deserts and on remote mountaintops — the Atacama, Mauna Kea, the Canary Islands — chasing darkness like a natural resource, which is exactly what it is. Even there, the view is compromised: satellite constellations drag bright threads through long photographic exposures. Some towns have pushed back. Flagstaff, Arizona, became the world's first International Dark Sky City in 2001, and hundreds of protected places now enforce ordinances requiring shielded fixtures and warm-colored bulbs. And whenever a total solar eclipse sweeps across a continent, and the stars emerge at noon, and traffic stops and grown strangers audibly weep, you learn something reassuring: the human appetite for the cosmos is intact. It has merely been starved.

Down at ground level, the casualties are nonhuman and mostly silent. To wildlife, our lights are not ambiance; they are weather. Consider the sea turtle, which has run the same playbook for a hundred million years: hatch, scramble toward the brighter horizon, reach the sea. For a hundred million years, the brighter horizon meant moonlight on open water. Beachfront development has reversed the physics. In Florida alone, tens of thousands of hatchlings each season crawl away from the ocean and toward the glow of condominiums, into roads and swimming pools. Migrating birds navigate by stars and moonlight, and on foggy nights the beams of tall buildings trap entire flocks in circles of exhaustion until they drop; collisions with lit structures kill hundreds of millions of birds a year in the United States. Moths evolved to steer by keeping celestial light at a fixed angle; a streetlamp holds its angle perfectly while staying a constant distance away, converting navigation into orbit and orbit into a death spiral. Coral reefs synchronize their spawning by the moon, and harbor lights scramble the signal. Even the ocean's depths, where sunlight never reaches, run on light — most animals down there make their own, flashing in precise, coded conversations. Nature's light is information. Ours, mostly, is noise.

Here is the encouraging twist, rare among environmental catastrophes: light pollution is solved by subtraction. Point the fixture down. Choose warm amber over blue-white. Put timers on empty office floors and motion sensors on garages. The result is lower bills, a darker sky, and — contrary to instinct — often *more* safety, because glare creates deep shadows in which trouble hides, and a blinding floodlight can serve an intruder better than a homeowner. Unlike carbon dioxide, darkness returns instantly. Flip the switch tonight and the sky begins coming back tonight.

* * *

So what was the darkness for? Partly, it was for scale. Stand under a genuinely pristine sky — the kind rated Class 1 on the astronomer's darkness scales, found now mainly in deserts and high oceans of grassland — and you discover that you are not looking *at* the galaxy. You are inside it, seeing its own disk edge-on as a river of pale fire, and the understanding lands in the body before the mind: the universe is not a ceiling but a depth. Artificial light makes the world legible. Darkness makes it fathomable. Van Gogh, from the barred window of his asylum room in Saint-Rémy in June 1889, could see the morning star burning over the cypresses and painted it into *The Starry Night*. Tonight, a child in most cities can count fewer stars than Van Gogh could see planets.

Darkness was also for interiority — the mind's private weather. Thought seems to need dusk the way some seeds need dark soil. The hypnagogic drift before sleep, the reverie between the first and second sleep, the storytelling that only works when faces dissolve and voices float: these were technologies of the inner life, and bright, flat, uniform illumination erodes them. A world fully lit is a world with nowhere to hide, including from yourself.

None of this argues for extinguishing civilization. It argues for editing it. Shield the lights. Warm the spectrum. Dim the empty districts after midnight, the way Chicago's McCormick Place found it could — and watched its bird deaths fall sharply. And then, at least once, travel to real darkness, somewhere far from any halo, and wait thirty minutes for your eyes to open fully. The Milky Way is dense enough there to cast a faint shadow. The photons landing on your skin left their stars before animals existed. Your shadow, in that place, is cast by the galaxy itself.

Remember Los Angeles, January 1994. The silvery cloud the callers reported had not appeared. It had been there all along, patient behind the sodium haze, waiting for one broken transformer to give it an opening. The dark was never emptiness. It is the rest of the universe — and it is still overhead, every clear night, asking almost nothing of us except that we look up.
